value.overview: The Sunbittern (Eurypyga helias) is a distinctive tropical American bird and the only species in its family, Eurypygidae. Despite its name and bittern-like shape, it is not a true bittern. It usually walks quietly beside streams and other freshwater habitats, where its cryptic plumage helps it remain unnoticed. When alarmed, it spreads its wings to reveal large, eye-like markings and bright orange, black, and yellow patterns that can startle predators.
value.classification: The Sunbittern belongs to the order Eurypygiformes and family Eurypygidae. It is the only living species in the genus Eurypyga, although several geographic subspecies are recognized.
value.identification: This medium-sized bird has a long neck, long legs, a pointed bill, and broad rounded wings. Its upperparts are finely patterned in gray, brown, and buff, providing excellent camouflage in shaded forest. The wings show bold rufous, black, yellow, and white markings when spread. Adults are usually about 43–48 cm long. In Costa Rica, it can be confused at a distance with a small heron, but its upright posture, terrestrial habits, and strongly patterned wings are distinctive.
value.rangeHabitat: The Sunbittern occurs from southern Mexico and Guatemala through Central America and into northern and western South America, reaching Brazil. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, reported mainly in humid lowland and foothill forests along clear streams, rivers, forest pools, and other quiet freshwater margins. It favors shaded banks with leaf litter, rocks, and dense vegetation, and may occur from the Caribbean slope to parts of the southern Pacific slope. It is generally localized and can be difficult to observe.
value.migrationStatus: The Sunbittern is generally resident and is not considered a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, birds are present year-round. Individuals may make local movements along watersheds or shift short distances during dry periods to remain near suitable permanent water.
value.breeding: Sunbitterns form territorial pairs and often breed near forest streams. The nest is a bulky structure made from vegetation, usually placed above the ground in a tree, shrub, or on a bank. The clutch commonly contains two eggs. Both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Nestlings are covered in down and remain dependent on their parents after hatching. Breeding biology has been studied in Costa Rica, where nesting is associated with wooded freshwater habitats.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small aquatic and terrestrial animals found along stream margins. Sunbitterns eat fish, frogs, tadpoles, aquatic insects, crustaceans, earthworms, and other invertebrates. They walk slowly while searching among wet leaf litter, shallow water, mud, and rocks, then seize prey with a quick movement of the bill. Their feeding areas are usually quiet, shaded banks rather than open wetlands or deep water.
value.behavior: Sunbitterns are secretive, slow-moving birds that usually forage alone or in pairs. They walk along stream edges and may remain motionless when approached, relying on camouflage. If threatened, a bird suddenly opens its wings, exposing conspicuous patterns that resemble large eyes; this defensive display may confuse or deter a predator. The species also gives soft calls and maintains territories, especially during the breeding season.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently classified as threatened.
